Surgeons have performed limb-lengthening procedures to correct existing discrepancies or growth irregularities for decades , but the 2020s have seen a surge in patients, often men, seeking the procedures with the sole purpose of increasing their height. Depending on the surgery type, patients can expect an increase of 3 to 6 inches—a potentially life-changing difference for those struggling with low self-esteem and perceived bias in the workplace and dating landscape. Somalia: Children facing deadly hunger as admissions for severe malnutrition nearly triple in six months
articles.description: Country: Somalia Source: Save the Children BAIDOA, Somalia, 29 July 2026 – The number of children receiving treatment for the most dangerous form of malnutrition in Baidoa, south central Somalia, nearly tripled in six months, according to new figures from Save the Children’s stabilization centre in the region [1], warning over the country’s worsening drought and hunger crisis. Health care workers at Save the Children's Baidoa stabilization centres treated 400 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition with other medical complications in June – nearly three times as many as the 143 admitted in January. In total, the stabilization centre treated 1,405 children between January and June 2026, a 177% increase compared with the 507 children treated a year ago. Poor rainfall, reduced harvests, livestock losses, reduced foreign aid, high food prices, and weaker household purchasing power is driving this worsening hunger crisis in Baidoa, said Save the Children. The deterioration in hunger and malnutrition also comes as Somalia marks 15 years since a famine was declared 20 July 2011, killing over 250,000 people, about half of them children under five. Admissions to the centre’s outpatient programme, which treats moderate acute malnutrition cases also saw a sharp 268% increase in the first four months of the year. However, stock-outs of ready-to-use therapeutic food and other essential supplies due to aid cuts and the conflict in the middle east has meant that families are no longer able to receive treatment and many have stopped going to the centre, Save the Children said, leading to a sharp decline in admissions from April onwards [2]. While faced with a worsening drought and hunger crisis, aid organizations are also grappling with steep funding shortfalls, with more than 300 nutrition facilities reportedly closed across Somalia this year [3], reducing access to treatment for vulnerable children and families. This has caused a dangerous decline in number of people receiving humanitarian assistance, with only 12% of people in need being reached [4]. In May, data from the global hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), showed that about half of children under 5 in Somalia are facing acute malnutrition with Burhakaba district in the Bay region of southwest Somalia classified to be facing the risk of famine through June 2026 – the first time such a classification has been announced in Somalia since the devastating drought of 2022. As well as hunger, disease outbreaks are multiplying the risks for children in Somalia, with the outbreaks of measles, cholera and acute watery diarrhoea worsening malnutrition among children. The Federal Government of Somalia declared a drought emergency in November 2025, its first such declaration since the country narrowly averted famine in 2022, but resources are still outpacing needs. Aisha*, 27, whose two-year-old daughter Ayan* was treated for severe acute malnutrition at the centre after the family was displaced by drought, said: "We used to depend on farming and livestock keeping. However, the drought affected our livelihoods and forced us to leave our home and move to Baidoa. "My two-year-old daughter, Ayan*, became seriously ill. Her illness began with a fever and later developed into diarrhoea and sores in her mouth. “When we first arrived, she was not eating anything. However, after receiving treatment, she began eating well. She even started asking for the food I was eating.” Mustaf, a doctor at the Save the Children-supported stabilisation centre in Baidoa, said: “This year, the number of children we are treating has doubled or even tripled compared with previous years, mainly because of the severe drought. Pastoralists have lost their livestock and farmers have suffered repeated crop failures. “We depend heavily on humanitarian assistance from organisations such as Save the Children. Should that assistance decrease, we will be unable to continue providing essential services. Medicines and equipment will run short, and many children whose lives could have been saved may not receive the treatment they need.” Mohamud Mohamed Hassan, Save the Children's Country Director in Somalia, said: “Fifteen years ago, the world watched Somalia's children die in a famine that early warnings failed to stop. Today those warnings are flashing again in the same regions, and the children reaching our centre in Baidoa are more severely ill than we have seen in years. “The difference between a warning and a tragedy is whether the response arrives in time. In 2011 it did not. We cannot let Bay Region's children pay that price twice.” “We know how to prevent this. What is missing is not knowledge but funding and speed. If assistance reaches Bay Region now, these children will recover and go home. If it comes late, we will be counting a cost we promised in 2011 never to repeat. The world now has to match that urgency.” Save the Children is calling for an urgent and sustained scale-up of food security, nutrition, health and water and sanitation assistance in Bay region and other hotspots, and for the funding needed to reach children before Burhakaba crosses the line into famine. Save the Children has worked in Somalia since 1951, delivering health, nutrition, education, child protection and emergency assistance for children and their families. END NOTES TO EDITORS: [1] Baidoa admissions figures are drawn from Save the Children's own programme data, January to June 2026, compared with the same period in 2025. [2] Cases to the outpatient programme: 1167 cases in April, 317 in May and 520 in June, caused by critical delays and stock-outs of ready-to-use therapeutic food and other essential supplies used in treatment. [3] Save the Children, “When Aid Disappears, Childhood Disappears Too” , 28 April 2026. [4] IPC Somalia Acute Food Insecurity and Acute Malnutrition Projection Update, April to June 2026, issued 14 May 2026: about half of children under five acutely malnourished; Burhakaba at risk of famine; humanitarian assistance reaching only 12 percent of people in IPC Phase 3 or above. ******************************************************************************************************************* For further enquiries please contact: Delfhin Mugo, Media Manager – Africa, based in NAIROBI Delfhin.Mugo@savethechildren.org Our media out of hours (GMT) contact is media@savethechildren.org.uk / +44(0)7831 650409 Please also check our X account @Save_GlobalNews for news alerts, quotes, statements and location Vlogs.

articles.title: World: Africa CDC and PSI Partner to Expand Innovative Approaches for Immunisation and Primary Healthcare Access in Africa
articles.description: Country: World Sources: Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, Population Services International Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 28 July 2026 – A new partnership agreement between the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and Population Services International (PSI) will strengthen efforts to expand access to immunisation and integrated primary healthcare services across Africa. The partnership brings together Africa CDC’s continental leadership in health security with PSI’s experience as a global health organisation working with governments, communities and partners to design and scale people-centred solutions that improve access to quality and affordable healthcare. Through the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by Africa CDC Director General Dr Jean Kaseya and PSI President Michael Holscher, the two organisations will collaborate on innovative approaches to preventive healthcare, including pharmacy-based immunisation community delivery models, stronger public-private partnerships, health workforce integration, evidence generation and knowledge exchange. The agreement comes as African countries continue efforts to close gaps in access to essential health services and build more resilient health systems capable of reaching communities with life-saving interventions. More than seven million children on the continent remain unvaccinated with routine vaccines while an additional 3.3 million started but did not complete the vaccination series, highlighting the need for innovative approaches that bring immunisation services closer to communities across the life course “Africa’s health security depends on our ability to ensure that every person can access life-saving preventive services,” said Dr Kaseya. “This partnership with PSI will help bring immunisation and primary healthcare closer to communities while strengthening national systems and building a healthier, more resilient Africa.” The collaboration supports Africa CDC’s mandate to strengthen disease prevention and control, enhance health security and advance stronger public health systems across the continent. The Africa CDC Strategic Plan (2023–2027) prioritises expanded access to vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics, strengthened public health institutions, a skilled health workforce and action-oriented partnerships to address Africa’s evolving health challenges. Under the agreement, Africa CDC and PSI will collaborate on regional and sub-regional knowledge exchange, policy engagement with ministries of health and immunisation stakeholders, dissemination of implementation evidence, long-term scale-up planning, and the development of platforms to document and share good practices across African Union Member States. A key area of collaboration will be advancing Pharmacy-Based Immunisation Delivery (PBID) models in line with national policies which aim to expand access to vaccination and preventive health services through diverse community-based platforms. The partnership will support Member States in integrating trained pharmacists and healthcare workers into national systems while generating evidence to inform policy and programme decisions. PSI will serve as the technical lead and implementing partner for the PBID initiative, supporting technical design, research, digital innovation, workforce development, stakeholder engagement, monitoring and evaluation and country-level implementation aligned with national priorities. Africa CDC will provide strategic advisory support, regional coordination, policy dialogue and convening support to facilitate knowledge exchange and sustainable scale-up across Member States. “No one should miss out on life-saving immunisation and preventive care because it is too far away or too difficult to access,” said Mr Holscher. “Together with Africa CDC, we will work alongside African governments to bring these essential services closer to where people live and work through innovative, locally-led solutions that strengthen primary healthcare systems and improve health outcomes for the long-term.” The two organisations will also establish mechanisms for continued coordination, including technical working groups to review progress, address policy and operational priorities, and identify opportunities for further cooperation. By combining Africa CDC’s continental mandate with PSI’s implementation expertise, the partnership will support African countries in strengthening innovative immunisation delivery, expanding access to primary healthcare services, and accelerating progress towards Universal Health Coverage. ### About Africa CDC The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is the autonomous public health agency of the African Union. It supports African Union Member States in preventing, detecting and responding rapidly and effectively to disease threats and public health emergencies while strengthening public health institutions and systems across the continent. About PSI PSI is a network of locally led, globally-connected organisations that are passionate about making it easier for people to lead healthier lives. PSI addresses diverse factors that affect people’s health and lives – from the effects of climate change to urbanisation, and limited livelihood opportunities – and leverages social marketing roots to scale social business models and reach people in new, impactful ways. Media contacts: Communications and Public Information Directorate, Africa CDC: communications@africacdc.org Taylor Prochnow, Head of Global Communications, PSI: TProchnow@psi.org

articles.title: World: From Prevention to Sovereignty: Accelerating Viral Hepatitis Elimination in Africa
articles.description: Country: World Source: Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention By Dr Jean Kaseya, Director General, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) Each year, World Hepatitis Day is more than a call for awareness; it is a call for action. As Africa advances its Health Security and Sovereignty agenda, viral hepatitis presents a critical opportunity to translate commitment into impact through stronger, self-reliant health systems. In line with the Cairo Declaration, African Union Member States are accelerating efforts to expand hepatitis prevention, testing, and treatment services across the continent. Despite being preventable and treatable, hepatitis B and C remain major causes of death, with Africa carrying one of the highest burdens globally. An estimated 64 million Africans live with chronic hepatitis B, yet only 6% know their status and fewer than 2% receive treatment. The challenge is no longer a lack of scientific solutions but a gap in implementation. Integrating hepatitis services into broader health systems and universal health coverage efforts is essential to closing this gap and achieving elimination targets. Science is already on our side. Effective tools exist to prevent, diagnose, and treat viral hepatitis. Timely hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination, safe blood supplies, infection prevention measures, expanded testing, and affordable antiviral treatment can dramatically reduce transmission, illness, and deaths. The priority now is to ensure these proven interventions reach every mother, every newborn, and every community through strong, integrated primary health care systems. Encouragingly, Africa’s hepatitis response is gaining momentum. Growing political commitment, scientific innovation, and regional collaboration are demonstrating that elimination is both achievable and affordable. When embedded within national health and development priorities rather than approached as a stand-alone disease programme, hepatitis elimination can become a powerful example of how Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty agenda delivers measurable health gains for its people. Africa no longer needs to look beyond the continent for proof that hepatitis elimination is achievable. Egypt’s landmark 100 Million Healthier Lives campaign, which screened over 50 million people and placed the country on the path to hepatitis C elimination, has become a global model. Rwanda has screened more than seven million people and expanded free hepatitis C treatment nationwide, while Uganda’s sustained domestic investment has enabled free hepatitis B testing, treatment, and viral load monitoring. Similar progress in Nigeria, Senegal, Ghana, and Cameroon underscores a common lesson: when political commitment is matched by domestic financing, innovation, and partnership, hepatitis elimination becomes a realistic and affordable goal. This momentum is increasingly being driven at the continental level. Nearly all Member States have integrated hepatitis B vaccination into routine childhood immunization programmes, and the African Union’s Plan Towards the Elimination of Vertical Transmission of HIV, Syphilis, and Hepatitis B by 2030 reflects a strong commitment to integrated maternal, newborn, and child health services. Complementing these efforts, Africa CDC’s Continental Viral Hepatitis Prevention and Control Programme has strengthened regional coordination, supported Member States in developing and improving national hepatitis programmes, and fostered collaboration among governments, scientific institutions, and civil society. Moreover, today, Africa CDC is launching a practical operational toolkit and digital decision-support platform that translates WHO hepatitis B guidelines into frontline action, helping bridge the gap between policy and implementation across all levels of healthcare delivery. Together, these achievements demonstrate that Africa is not only committed to hepatitis elimination; it is already building the systems, partnerships, and leadership needed to achieve it. Despite the progress, significant challenges remain. Across Africa, only 17% of newborns receive the life-saving hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours of birth, while many pregnant women are still not screened for hepatitis B during antenatal care. As a result, millions of people remain undiagnosed until they present with advanced liver disease or liver cancer. These gaps reflect not only missed opportunities for prevention and early treatment but also broader health system weaknesses in service delivery, diagnostics, financing, and continuity of care. Addressing them requires positioning viral hepatitis as a strategic priority within Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty agenda, leveraging hepatitis elimination as a catalyst for stronger, more resilient, and more equitable health systems. Call to Action Investing in viral hepatitis elimination therefore strengthens far more than health outcomes. It protects workforce productivity, reduces long-term health expenditure, strengthens economic resilience and advances sustainable development. Accelerating elimination requires the very capabilities that define AHSS: resilient primary health care, integrated surveillance and laboratory networks, predictable domestic financing, digital transformation, stronger regional cooperation, local manufacturing and pooled procurement mechanisms. Therefore, as we observe World Hepatitis Day, we urge our Member States and partners to enhance our response efforts in these five critical areas: Increase domestic financing and innovative funding mechanisms to expand hepatitis prevention, testing, and treatment while reducing reliance on external aid. African governments should explore new sources of domestic and blended financing, including solidarity levies, health security bonds, diaspora bonds, sin taxes, and catalytic private-sector investment, to complement public financing. Strengthen local manufacturing and pooled procurement of vaccines, diagnostics, and antiviral medicines to improve access, affordability, and supply security. Integrate hepatitis services into primary health care and digital health systems, ensuring that every newborn receives timely hepatitis B vaccination and every diagnosed person is linked to care and treatment. Deepen regional cooperation and partnerships to share expertise, scale proven interventions, and sustain momentum toward the 2030 elimination targets. Promote public awareness and community engagement to reduce stigma, increase demand for testing, and improve vaccine uptake. Civil society and community organizations should be engaged as key partners in elimination efforts.
